title: A Model Predictive Control-Inspired Quantum Algorithm
authors: Dominic Messina, Alicia B. Magann, Mohan Sarovar, Helen Durand
abstract: We introduce a new hybrid quantum-classical algorithm inspired by an advanced control strategy known as model predictive control (MPC). This algorithm unifies the optimization-based design of variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) with the feedback-based design of feedback-based quantum algorithms (FQAs). Variational circuit parameters are optimized using a layer-wise receding horizon strategy, where observable measurements after every layer initialize a classically simulated dynamic model used to predict quantum state evolution and optimize over future parameterized gates. This hybrid algorithm can be used for applications such as ground state preparation and approximate combinatorial optimization, and presents an ideal use case for the integration of quantum computers with high-performance computing, where the latter resource can be used to increase the scale and efficiency of the predictions critical to MPC. We show through mathematical proof and numerical evidence that the MPC-based algorithm can be guaranteed to at least match the performance of FQAs. Through simulations on Max-Cut problems and a two-dimensional transverse-field Ising model, we demonstrate that relaxed implementations of the MPC-based algorithm can also provide improved performance in practice compared to an FQA.
summary: This paper introduces an MPC-inspired hybrid quantum algorithm that merges the optimization strengths of VQAs with the feedback nature of FQAs for quantum computation. It uses a receding horizon approach, where classical simulation predicts future state evolution to optimize gate parameters layer by layer. The method successfully demonstrates superior or comparable performance to existing algorithms on key optimization models.
main_problem: The paper addresses the need for an advanced quantum algorithm that surpasses the limitations of existing Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) and Feedback-Based Quantum Algorithms (FQAs). It proposes a Model Predictive Control (MPC)-inspired hybrid approach to optimize quantum circuit design.
main_result: The MPC-based algorithm is mathematically proven to match or exceed the performance of FQAs, and simulations show it can provide improved practical results for optimization tasks like Max-Cut and TFIM.
method: It employs a layer-wise receding horizon strategy, using classical simulation initialized by observable measurements after each quantum circuit layer to predict future state evolution and optimize subsequent gate parameters.
model_or_system: The algorithm is applied to solving optimization problems (e.g., Max-Cut) defined by a problem Hamiltonian ($H_p$). The underlying dynamics are governed by time evolution under a total Hamiltonian $H(t) = H_p + H_d  eta(t)$.
key_observables: The primary observable is the expectation value of the problem Hamiltonian, $\langle H_p angle$, which the algorithm seeks to minimize.
important_parameters: Key parameters include the prediction horizon ($N$), the time step ($\Delta t$), and the gate control parameters ($ eta$).
main_assumptions: The primary limitation is the computational intractability of the full optimization problem due to the need for state vector simulation, necessitating reduced-order models.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate $\langle H_p angle$ trajectories comparing MPC and FALQON on Max-Cut and TFIM; Figure 13 specifically shows the prediction vs. actual evolution using the receding horizon policy.
paper_structure: The paper reviews background (FALQON, MPC), details the quantum algorithm construction using MPC concepts, discusses necessary computational simplifications via reduced-order models, and concludes with numerical simulations on benchmark problems.
why_interesting: For AMO/open systems researchers, this work provides a novel framework for controlling complex quantum dynamics by integrating predictive control theory. The focus on optimizing time evolution paths ($\langle H_p angle$ minimization) using feedback mechanisms is highly relevant to open system control.
